title: Arteries of the hand (palmar)
attribution: 3D anatomy from Z-Anatomy, built on BodyParts3D (CC BY-SA). Rendered in Blender, with surface detail added by an image model.

rows: Arises from
Brachial artery, in the cubital fossa at the level of the neck of the radius. It is the smaller end branch.
Course

Runs down the lateral side of the forearm under brachioradialis and at the wrist lies on the radius, lateral to the tendon of flexor carpi radialis, where the radial pulse is felt. It then winds around the lateral side of the wrist, across the floor of the anatomical snuffbox, and passes between the two heads of the first dorsal interosseous muscle into the palm.
Supplies
Lateral side of the forearm, the wrist, the thumb, and the lateral side of the index finger. It ends as the main part of the deep palmar arch.
hy: Allen test: the person makes a tight fist while both arteries are pressed at the wrist. The hand is opened, pale, and the ulnar artery is released. If the hand does not turn pink within a few seconds, the ulnar artery may not supply the hand alone, and the radial artery should not be cannulated or removed.

rows: Arises from
Brachial artery, in the cubital fossa at the level of the neck of the radius. It is the larger end branch.
Course

Passes deep to pronator teres and the superficial flexor muscles to the medial side of the forearm, then runs down beside flexor carpi ulnaris with the ulnar nerve on its medial side. It enters the hand in front of the flexor retinaculum, just lateral to the pisiform.
Supplies
Medial side of the forearm and, through the common interosseous artery, the deep muscles of the front and back of the forearm. It ends as the main part of the superficial palmar arch.
Arises from
Mainly the ulnar artery, of which it is the continuation. It is usually completed on the lateral side by a branch of the radial artery, typically the superficial palmar branch.
Course

Curves across the palm just under the palmar aponeurosis, in front of the long flexor tendons, at about the level of the distal border of the outstretched thumb. It lies nearer the fingers than the deep palmar arch.
Supplies
Fingers, through three common palmar digital arteries and a branch to the medial side of the little finger.
Arises from
Mainly the radial artery, of which it is the continuation. It is completed on the medial side by the deep palmar branch of the ulnar artery.
Course

Enters the palm between the two heads of adductor pollicis and curves across the bases of the metacarpals, deep to the long flexor tendons, with the deep branch of the ulnar nerve. It lies about a finger's breadth nearer the wrist than the superficial arch.
Supplies

Gives three palmar metacarpal arteries, perforating branches to the back of the hand, and small branches to the wrist. The arteries of the thumb and of the lateral side of the index finger leave the radial artery just as the arch begins.
Arises from
Superficial palmar arch. There are three.
Course

Run toward the fingers on the second, third, and fourth lumbrical muscles. Near the webs of the fingers each is joined by a palmar metacarpal artery from the deep arch and divides into two proper palmar digital arteries.
Supplies
Through their branches, the facing sides of the index, middle, ring, and little fingers.
Arises from

Mostly the common palmar digital arteries, each of which divides into two. The one to the medial side of the little finger comes straight from the superficial palmar arch, and those of the thumb and the lateral side of the index finger come from the radial artery.
Course
One runs along each side of every finger, beside the palmar digital nerve, to the fingertip.
Supplies
The finger: skin, flexor tendons, joints, and, through dorsal branches, the back of the middle and distal phalanges with the nail bed.
Arises from
Deep palmar arch. There are three.
Course
Run toward the fingers on the interosseous muscles of the second, third, and fourth spaces and join the common palmar digital arteries near the webs of the fingers.
Supplies
Interosseous muscles and metacarpal bones. They also carry blood from the deep arch to the arteries of the fingers.
